intro: Orthogonal means at right angles. This branch uses right angles to find closest points and best approximations, which underlies fitting a line to messy data.

VII.8.01.what: An inner product is a way of multiplying vectors to measure length and angle. The dot product is the standard one.

levels.a: Uses the dot product on lists of any length.
levels.b: Finds lengths and distances from it.
levels.c: Works with other inner products, such as ones for functions.
levels.d: Uses the rules every inner product must follow.

VII.8.02.what: Two vectors are orthogonal when they meet at a right angle, which happens exactly when their dot product is zero.

levels.a: Tests for a right angle by checking the dot product is zero.
levels.b: Uses the Pythagorean theorem for perpendicular vectors in any dimension.
levels.c: Tests whether every pair in a set is perpendicular.
levels.d: Finds a vector perpendicular to given ones.

VII.8.03.what: The orthogonal complement of a subspace is every vector at right angles to all of it, like the vertical line beneath a flat floor.

levels.c: Shows the row space and null space are perpendicular to each other.
levels.d: Uses the fact that the two dimensions add up to the whole.

VII.8.04.what: An orthogonal basis is a set of building-block vectors that are all at right angles to each other, which makes calculations much easier.

levels.a: Shows perpendicular nonzero vectors are automatically independent.
levels.b: Finds coordinates quickly using dot products.
levels.c: Checks whether a set is an orthogonal basis.
levels.d: Explains why such bases save so much work.

VII.8.05.what: An orthonormal basis has perpendicular vectors that are also each of length 1, the tidiest possible basis.

levels.b: Checks a matrix's columns are orthonormal by one multiplication.
levels.c: Finds coordinates instantly using dot products.
levels.d: Shows these coordinates keep lengths unchanged.

VII.8.06.what: Projecting onto a subspace finds the nearest point in it, like dropping a straight shadow onto a floor.

levels.a: Uses the projection formula with a perpendicular basis.
levels.c: Splits a vector into a part in the subspace and a perpendicular part.
levels.d: Builds a matrix that performs the projection.

VII.8.07.what: The best approximation theorem says the projection is the closest point in the subspace to a given vector.

levels.b: Finds the distance from a vector to a subspace.
levels.c: Computes the closest point in examples.
levels.d: Explains why the projection beats every other point.

VII.8.08.what: Gram–Schmidt is a step-by-step recipe for turning any basis into one where every vector is at right angles to the rest.

levels.a: Learns the key move: subtract the shadow on earlier vectors.
levels.b: Runs the process on two vectors.
levels.d: Scales the results to length 1 at the end.

VII.8.09.what: QR factorization splits a matrix into a part with perpendicular columns and a triangular part, a standard tool in computing.

levels.a: Builds the perpendicular-column part using Gram–Schmidt.
levels.b: Finds the triangular part by a single multiplication.
levels.c: Checks the factors multiply back to the original.

VII.8.10.what: Least squares finds the best approximate solution when a system has no exact one, keeping the total error as small as possible.

levels.a: Recognizes systems with no exact solution.
levels.b: Sets up the normal equations, a solvable related system.
levels.c: Solves them for the best approximate answer.
levels.d: Measures how large the leftover error is.

VII.8.11.what: Fitting the best straight line or curve through scattered data points, the method behind a trend line on a chart.

levels.a: Sets up the design matrix from the data.
levels.c: Fits curves, such as a parabola, to data.
levels.d: Connects this to regression in statistics.

VII.8.12.what: An orthogonal matrix moves things without distorting them, keeping every length and angle the same, like a rotation or mirror.

levels.a: Recognizes matrices whose columns are perpendicular and of length 1.
levels.b: Finds the inverse simply by transposing.
levels.c: Shows these matrices keep lengths and angles unchanged.
levels.d: Identifies them as rotations and reflections.
